many mnocent householders), who had no intention of 
breaking the law, would be trapped; and this seems 
to be the ratio decidendi in the decision of the Bombay 
High Court in Hub/al Kamtaprasad v. Goel Bros. & 
Co. Ltd. (Appeal No. 14 of 1950) which is the deci-
sion virtually, though not directly, under appeal here, 
though the learned Judges also take into consideration 
two further facts, namely that the law should be con-
strued in favour of the freedom of contracts ·and a 
penal enactment in favour of the subject. 
The English decision about tea just cited is to be 
contrasted with another decision, also about tea, 
given a few months later in same year: Sainsbury 
v. Saunders('). Two of the Judges, Darling and 
Avary, JJ. were parties to the earlier decision; Salter J. 
was not. He held that though tea 'had been held in 
the earlier case not to be a "food" for the purpose of 
the Food Hoarding Order of 1917, it was a "food" 
within the meaning of the expressions used in certain 
Defence of the Realm Regulations read with the New 
Ministries and Secretaries Act of 1916 which empower-
ed the Food Controller to regulate "the food supply of 
the country" and the "supply and consumption and 
production of food." Avary J. also considered that tea 
was an article of food for the purposes of rhese laws 
though Darling J. preferred to adhere to his earlier 
view. All three Judges also held that the provisions 
were wide enough to enable the Food Controller to hit 
at articles which were not food at all, such as sacks 
and tin containers (Darling J.) so long as he was able 
by these means even indirectly to regulate the supply 
of "food", but that portion of the decision does not 
concern us hen; because the laws they were inter-
preting were more widely phrased. 
Now the comparison of one Act with another is 
dangerous, especially when the Act used for com-
parison is an English Act and a war-time measure, 
and I have no intention of falling into that error. I 
am concerned here with the Act before me and must

interpret its provisions uninfluenced by expressions, 
however similar, used in other Acts. I have referred 
to the cases discussed above, not for purposes of com-
parison but to show that the terms "food" and "food-
~tuffs" can be used in both a wide and a narrow sense 
and that the circumstanct:l\ and background can alone 
determine which is proper in any given case. 
Turning to the Act with which we are concerned, it 
will be necessary again to advert to its history. Rule 
81 (2) was wide and all embracing and the Order of 
1944 clearly fell within its ambit. It is also relevant 
to note that one of the purposes of the Order, as dis;. 
closed in its preamble, was to "maintain supplies 
essential to the life of the community." As turmeric 
was specifically included with certain other spices, 
it is clear that turmeric was then considered tCJ be 
a commodity essential to the life of the community, 
that is to say, it wa& considered an essential com-
modity and not merely a luxury which at a time of 
austerity could be dispensed with. 
Then, when we turn to the Ordinance and the Act 
of 1946, we find from the preamble that the legislature 
considered that it was still necessary-
"to provide for the continuance . ....... of powers-to con-
trol the production, supply and distribution of, and 
trade and commerce in, foodstuffs . ... " 
Section 3(1) of the Act continues this theme: 
"The Central Government, so far as it appears to 
it to be necessary or expedient for maintaining or 
increasing supplies of any essential commodity, or for 
securing their equitable distribution and availability 
at fair prices, may by notified order provide for 
regulating or prohibiting the production, supply and 
distribution thereof and trade and commerce therein." 
The Ordinance is in the same terms. 
Now I have no doubt that had the Central Govern-
ment re-promulgated the Order of 1944 in 1946 after 
the passing of either the Ordinance of the Act of 1946, 
the Order would have been good. As we have seen, 
turmeric falls within the wider definition of "food"

and "foodstuffs" given in a dictionary of international 
standing as well as in several English decisions. It is, 
I think, as much a "foodstuff'', in its wider meaning, 
as sausage, skins and baking powder and tea. In the 
face of all that I would find it difficult to hold that, an 
article like turmeric cannot fall within the wider 
meaning of the term "foodstuffs". Had the Order of 
1944 not specified turmeric and had it merely pro-
hibited forward oontracts in "foddstuffs" I would have 
held, in line with the earlier tea case, that that is not 
a proper way of penalising a man for trading in an 
article which would. not ordinarily be considered as a 
foodstuff. But in the face of the order of 1944, which 
specifically includes turmeric, no one can oomplain 
that his attention was not drawn to the prohibition of 
trading in this particular commodity and if, in spite 
of that, he chooses to disregard the Order and test its 
validity in a court of law, he can hardly complain 
that he was •trapped or taken unawares; whatever he 
may have thought he was at any rate placed on his 
guard. As I see it, the test here is whether the Order 
of 1944 would have been a good order had it been re-
promulgated after the Ordinance of 1946. In my 
opinion, it would, and from that it follows that it is 
saved by the saving clauses of· the Ordinance and the 
Act. 
I have already set out section 5 of the Ordinance. 
In my opinion, ·the Order of 1944 falls within its pur-
view, and if it is saved by thait, i!t is equally saved 
by section 17 (2) of the Act. The section is in these 
terms: 
"Any order . . . . . . . . . . deemed to be made under the 
said Ordinance and in force immediately before the 
commencement of this Act shall continue in force and 
be deemed to be an order made under this Act." 
In my opinion, the conviction was good and the High 
Court was wrong in setting it aside, but though the

BosE J.-The question in this case is whether

The respondent was charged with having contra-

into a forward contract in turmeric at Sangli on the 
18th of March, 1950, in contravention of clause 3 of the 
Order. He was convicted by the trial Court and sen-

months. But he was acquitted on appeal by the 
Sessions Court. An appeal to the High Court against 
the acquittal failed. 
The State of Bombay appeals here but makes 1t 
plain that it does not want to take any further steps 
against the respondent in this matter but merely 
wants to have the question of law decided as a test 
case as the judgment of the Bombay High Court will 
have far-reaching effects in the State of Bombay. 
It will be necessary to trace the history of this 
legislation. In the year 1944 the then Central Govern-
ment of India promulgated the Spices (Forward Con-
tracts Prohibition) Order, 1944, under Rule 81(2) of 
the Defence of India Rules. Clauses 2 and 3 read to-
gether prohibited forward contracts in any of the 
"spices" specified in the first cdlumn of the schedule 
to that Order. Among the artides listed in the 
schedule was turmeric. The conviction is under that 
Order and it is admitted that if that Order is still 
valid the conviction would be good. 
The Defence of India Act was due to expire on the 
30th of September, 1946, and with it the Spices Order 
of 1944. But before it expired an Ordinance called

Section 5 of this Ordinance embodied a •aving

"Any order ...... made ...... under rule 81(2) of the .. _ ..

The Ordinance was later replaced by the Act with

The Act merely reproduces the language of the Ordi,

The appellant's contention is that turmeric is a

is, is turmeric a "foodstuff"?_

what is and what is not a foodstuff; and the only con-

is limited to articles which are eaten as food for pur-

my opinion, the problem posed cannot be answered in 
the abstract and must be viewed in relation to its 
background and context. But before I dilate on this, I 
will exa1nine the dictionary meaning of the words. 
The Oxford English Dictionary defines "foodstuff" 
as follows: 
"that which is taken into the system to maintain 
life and growth and to supply waste of tissue." 
In Webster's International Dictionary "food" is 
defined as: 
"nutritive material absorbed or taken into the

"Animals differ greatly from plants in their nutri-

which fall into three principal groups, Proteins,

" As used in laws prohibiting adulteration etc.,

"foodstuff" is anything which is used as "food". 
So far as "food" is concerned, it can be used in a 
wlde as well a narrow sense and, ,1n my opm10n, 
much must depend upon the context and background. 
Even in a popular sense, when one asks another, "Have 
you had your food?", one means the composite prepa-

and rice, sweetmeats, pudding, cooked vegetables and 
so forth. One does not usually think separately of the 
different preparaticms which enter into their making, 
of the various condiments and spices and vitamins, 
any mme than one woukl think of separating in his 
mind the purely nutritive elements of what is eaten 
from their non-nutritive adjuncts. 
So also, looked at from another point of view, the 
various adjuncts of what I may term food proper which 
enter into its preparation for human consumption in 
order to make it palatable and nutritive, can hardly 
be separated from the purely nutritive elements if the 
effect of their absence would' be to render the parti-
cular commodity i:n its finished state unsavoury and 
indigestible to a whole class of persons whose stomachs 
are accustomed to a more spicely prepared product. 
The proof of the pudding is, as it were, in the eating, 
and if the effect of eating what would otherwise be 
palatable and digestible and therefore nutrhive is to 
bring on indigestion to a stomach unaccustomed to 
to such unspiced fare, the answer must, I think, be 
that however nutritive a· product may be in one form

the essense of the definition is the nutritive ele-

The prosecution there was directed against an

The Constitution (First Amendment) 'Act, 1951, which has 
inserted, inter alia, Arts. 31A and 31B in the Constitution of 
India is riot ultra vires or unconstitutional. 
The provisional Parliament is competent to exercise the power 
of amending the Constitution under Art. 368. The fact that the 
said article refers to the two Houses of the Parliament and the 
President separately and not to the Parliament, does not lead to 
the inference that the body which is invested with the power to 
amend is not the Parliament but a different body consisting of 
the two Houses. . 
The words "all the powers confer{ed by the provisions of this 
Constitution ori Parliament': in Art. 379 are not confined to such 
powers as could be exercised by · the provisional Parliament con-
sisting of a single chamber, but are wide enough to include the 
power to amend the Constitution conferred by Art. 368. 
The Constitution (Removal of Difficulties} Order No. 2 made 
by the President on the 26th January, 1950, which purports to 
adapt Art. 368 · by omitting "either House of" and "in each 
House" and substituting "Parliament" for "that House" is not

There is nothing in Art. 392 to suggest that the President should 
wait, before adapting a particular article, till the oc.casion

The view that Art. 368 is a complete code in itself in respect 
of the procedure provided by it and does not contemplate any 
ainendment of a Bill for amendment of the Constitution after it 
has been introduced, and that if the Bill is amended during its 
passage through the House, the amendment Act cannot be said 
to have been passed in conformity with the procedure prescribed 
by Art. 368 and would be invalid, is erroneous. 
Although "Ia,v" must ordinarily include constitutional law 
there is a clear demarcation between ordinary law tvhich is made 
in the exercise of legislative power and constitutional law, 
which is made in the exercise of constituent power. In. the 
context of Art. 13, "law" must'be taken to mean rules or regula-
tions made in exercise of ordinary legislative po\ver and not 
amendments to the constitution made in the exercise of consti-
tuent power with the result that Art. 13(2) does not affect amend-
ments made under Art. 368. 
Articles 31A and 31B inserted in the Constitution by the 
Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, do not curtail the 
powers of the High Court under Art. 226 to issue writs for 
enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III or of the 
Supreme Court under Arts. 132 and 136 to entertain appeals 
from orders issuing or refusing such writs; but they only exclude 
from the purvie\v of Part III certain classes of cases. These 
articles therefore do not require ratification under cl. (b) of the 
proviso to Art. 368. 
Articles 3!A and 31B are not invalid on the ground that they 
relate to land \vhich is a matter covered by the State List (item 
18 of List II) as these articles are essentially amendments of the 
Constitution, and Parliament alone has the power to enact 
them.

PATANJALI SASTRI J.-These petitions, . which have 
been heard together, raise the common question 
whether the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, 
which .w~ recently passed by the present provisional 
Parliament and purports to insert, inter alia, articles 
31A. and 31B in the Constitution of India is ultra vires 
and unconstitutional. 
What led to that enactment is a matter of common 
knowledge. The political party now. in power, com-
manding as it does a majority -of votes in the several 
State legislatures' as well as in Parliament, carried out 
certain measures of agrarian reform in_ Bihar, Uttar 
Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh by enacting legislation 
which may cpmpendiously be referred to a.S Zemindary 
Abolition Acts. Certain zemindars, feeling themselves 
aggrieved, attacked the validity of those Acts in courts 
of law on the ground that they contravened · the fun-
damental rights conferred . on them by Part III of the 
Constitution. The High Court at Patna held that the 
Act passed ·in Bihar was unconstitutional while the

The provisional Parliament is competent to exercise the power

the inference that the body which is invested with the power to

the two Houses. .

Articles 31A and 31B inserted in the Constitution by the

Articles 3!A and 31B are not invalid on the ground that they

18 of List II) as these articles are essentially amendments of the 
Constitution, and Parliament alone has the power to enact

title: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala (1973)
case_name: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala
facts: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act which restricted religious mutt property ownership, challenging the constitutional validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments under Article 368.
issues: What is the extent of Parliament's amending power under Article 368?
Can Parliament abrogate or alter the fundamental structure of the Constitution?
ratio_decidendi: Parliament has wide constituent amending power under Article 368 but cannot alter the 'Basic Structure' or essential features of the Indian Constitution. The Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.
verdict: Upheld 24th Amendment; partially struck down Article 31C; established the landmark Basic Structure Doctrine.

title: Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965)
case_name: Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan
facts: Challenge to the 17th Amendment Act which added diverse State land reform acts into the Ninth Schedule.
issues: Can Fundamental Rights be amended under Article 368?
Did the 17th Amendment require state ratification under the Article 368 proviso?

verdict: Upheld 17th Amendment, but sowed the conceptual seeds for Golak Nath and Basic Structure.

title: I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967)
case_name: I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab
acts_referred: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953
facts: Family of Golak Nath held 500 acres of land. State declared excess land surplus under land reforms act. Family challenged 17th Amendment as abridging fundamental property rights.
issues: Is a constitutional amendment a 'law' under Article 13(2)?

ratio_decidendi: Fundamental Rights hold a transcendental and immutable position. Constitutional amendments under Article 368 are 'law' under Article 13(2). Parliament has no power to abridge Fundamental Rights. Applied Doctrine of Prospective Overruling.

title: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
case_name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
facts: Allahabad High Court invalidated Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's election for corrupt electoral practices. Parliament enacted the 39th Amendment inserting Article 329A(4) placing election of PM and Speaker beyond judicial review.
issues: Does Article 329A(4) violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution?
ratio_decidendi: First direct application of Basic Structure Doctrine. Democracy, rule of law, equality (Article 14), and judicial review are basic features. A constitutional amendment placing an individual's election beyond judicial scrutiny violates the Basic Structure.
verdict: Struck down Article 329A(4) inserted by the 39th Amendment; upheld election on statutory merits.

title: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
case_name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
facts: Minerva Mills challenged nationalization and the 42nd Amendment which added clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368 asserting unlimited amending power and expanded Article 31C to subordinate Fundamental Rights to all Directive Principles.
issues: Can Parliament grant itself unlimited amending power under Article 368?
Can Directive Principles take blanket precedence over Fundamental Rights?
ratio_decidendi: Limited amending power is itself a Basic Feature of the Constitution; Parliament cannot convert limited power into unlimited power. The harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is an essential basic feature.
verdict: Struck down Section 55 (Article 368(4)-(5)) and Section 4 (blanket Article 31C) of 42nd Amendment.

title: Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981)
case_name: Waman Rao v. Union of India
acts_referred: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961
facts: Challenge to agricultural land ceiling acts included in the Ninth Schedule and the constitutional validity of Articles 31A, 31B, and 31C.
issues: Does the Basic Structure doctrine apply to laws placed in the Ninth Schedule?

title: I.R. Coelho (Dead) By LRs v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)
case_name: I.R. Coelho (Dead) By LRs v. State of Tamil Nadu
facts: Referred to 9-judge bench to definitively resolve whether statutes placed in the Ninth Schedule after Kesavananda Bharati are completely immunized from judicial review for violating Fundamental Rights.
issues: Can Parliament insulate statutes violating Fundamental Rights from judicial review by putting them in Ninth Schedule?
ratio_decidendi: All laws placed in Ninth Schedule post-April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review using the 'Rights Test' and 'Essence of Rights Test'. If a Ninth Schedule statute violates the principles underlying Articles 14, 19, or 21, it damages the Basic Structure and will be void.
verdict: Unanimously affirmed that Ninth Schedule cannot be used as a constitutional black hole to bypass the Basic Structure.

NEUTRAL CITATION: 2007INSC28 | REPORTED CITATION: (2007) 2 SCC 1
COURT: Supreme Court of India | BENCH: 9-Judge Constitution Bench (Unanimous 9:0)
ARTICLES REFERRED: Article 31B, Ninth Schedule, Article 14, Article 19, Article 21, Article 32
STATUTES REFERRED: Gudalur Janmam Estates Act, 1969, West Bengal Land Reforms Act
FACTS & PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Referred to 9-judge bench to definitively resolve whether statutes placed in the Ninth Schedule after Kesavananda Bharati are completely immunized from judicial review for violating Fundamental Rights.
ISSUES / QUESTIONS OF LAW: ['Can Parliament insulate statutes violating Fundamental Rights from judicial review by putting them in Ninth Schedule?']
RATIO DECIDENDI: All laws placed in Ninth Schedule post-April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review using the 'Rights Test' and 'Essence of Rights Test'. If a Ninth Schedule statute violates the principles underlying Articles 14, 19, or 21, it damages the Basic Structure and will be void.
VERDICT & DISPOSITION: Unanimously affirmed that Ninth Schedule cannot be used as a constitutional black hole to bypass the Basic Structure.

title: Hussainara Khatoon & Ors. v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar (1979)
case_name: Hussainara Khatoon & Ors. v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
facts: Kapila Hingorani filed PIL highlighting tens of thousands of undertrial prisoners languishing in Bihar jails for periods exceeding maximum statutory sentences awaiting trial.
issues: Is the right to a speedy trial a fundamental right under Article 21?

title: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi (1981)
case_name: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
facts: British national detained under COFEPOSA was denied permission to meet family members and legal counsel under stringent prison restrictions.
issues: What is the scope of 'life' under Article 21?
Does Article 21 guarantee the right to live with human dignity?
ratio_decidendi: Article 21 guarantees something more than mere animal existence or physical survival. It includes the right to live with human dignity and all that goes with it, including bare necessities of life, nutrition, clothing, shelter, facilities for reading, and free intercourse with family.
verdict: Held harsh interview restrictions invalid; established dignity as core content of Article 21.

title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)
case_name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
facts: PIL petition letter by Executive Chairman, Legal Aid Services West Bengal, drawing attention to frequent custodial deaths and police brutality.
issues: What guidelines must be formulated to prevent custodial violence and safeguard arrested persons under Articles 21 and 22?
ratio_decidendi: Custodial violence, torture, and custodial deaths strike at the heart of the rule of law. Formulated 11 binding guidelines (memo of arrest, informing relative, medical examination every 48 hours, right to meet lawyer, display at control room) that must be strictly observed during arrest and detention.
verdict: Laid down mandatory D.K. Basu Guidelines on arrest; failure makes police officers liable for contempt of court.

title: Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010)
case_name: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
facts: Appellants challenged involuntary administration of neuro-scientific investigative techniques: Narco-analysis (sodium pentothal), Polygraph test (lie detector), and Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP).
issues: Does involuntary narco-analysis violate self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and mental privacy under Article 21?
ratio_decidendi: Involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraphy, and brain mapping constitutes testimonial compulsion violating Article 20(3) and infringes personal liberty and mental privacy under Article 21. Tests can only be administered voluntarily with informed consent.
verdict: Declared non-consensual narco-analysis and lie detector tests unconstitutional.

title: Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011)
case_name: Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v. Union of India
facts: Aruna Shanbaug, a nurse at KEM Hospital Mumbai, remained in a permanent vegetative state (PVS) for 37 years following a brutal sexual assault. Journalist Pinki Virani filed a writ petition seeking withdrawal of life support.
issues: Does Article 21 encompass the right to die with dignity?
Is passive euthanasia permissible under Indian constitutional law?
ratio_decidendi: Differentiated active euthanasia (administering lethal injection, prohibited) from passive euthanasia (withholding artificial life-support). Legalized passive euthanasia subject to strict High Court approval and medical board evaluation under the parens patriae doctrine.
verdict: Permitted passive euthanasia under judicial supervision; declined withdrawal for Aruna as KEM staff wished to care for her.

title: Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India (2018)
case_name: Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India
facts: Common Cause filed PIL seeking legal recognition of 'living wills' (advance medical directives) enabling terminally ill patients to refuse artificial life prolongation.
issues: Is the right to die with dignity part of Article 21?
Are advance medical directives / living wills legally enforceable?
ratio_decidendi: Right to die with dignity is an inseparable facet of the fundamental right to live with dignity under Article 21. An adult person of sound mind has bodily autonomy to execute an Advance Medical Directive refusing artificial life support when death is imminent.
verdict: Unanimously recognized Living Wills and advance medical directives; laid down simplified procedural safeguards.

title: M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (1954)
case_name: M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra
facts: Search warrants issued in Dalmia Group fraud investigation. Petitioners claimed search and seizure of private documents violated Article 19(1)(f) and Article 20(3).
issues: Does the Indian Constitution guarantee a fundamental right to privacy analogous to the US Fourth Amendment?
ratio_decidendi: The Indian Constitution does not contain any fundamental right to privacy analogous to the American Fourth Amendment. Search and seizure by police is not testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3).
verdict: Rejected constitutional right to privacy (later overruled in Puttaswamy).

title: Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1963)
case_name: Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
facts: Kharak Singh, acquitted in a dacoity case, was subjected to police surveillance: secret picketing, domiciliary night visits, and verification of movements under U.P. Police Regulations.
issues: Does police surveillance and domiciliary night visits violate fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(d) and 21?
ratio_decidendi: Majority held domiciliary night visits violate personal liberty under Article 21 (a person's house is their castle), but held privacy is not a guaranteed fundamental right. Subba Rao, J. dissented, prophetically writing that privacy is an essential ingredient of personal liberty.
verdict: Struck down night visits; majority denied comprehensive right to privacy.

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Privacy Judgment) (2017)
case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Privacy Judgment)
facts: Retired High Court Judge K.S. Puttaswamy challenged the mandatory Aadhaar biometric identification program. The Attorney General argued that under M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1963), the Constitution guaranteed no fundamental right to privacy.
issues: Is there a fundamental right to privacy under the Indian Constitution?
Are M.P. Sharma (8 judges) and Kharak Singh (6 judges) good law?
ratio_decidendi: Privacy is an intrinsic, fundamental, and inalienable right emanating from life and personal liberty under Article 21 and the entire schema of Part III. Privacy encompasses bodily autonomy, informational privacy, and spatial privacy. Any state interference must pass the three-fold test of: (1) legality (state law), (2) legitimate state aim, and (3) proportionality.
verdict: Unanimously upheld Right to Privacy as a Fundamental Right under Article 21; overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they held otherwise; explicitly denounced ADM Jabalpur.

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Aadhaar Validity) (2018)
case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Aadhaar Validity)
acts_referred: Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016
facts: Substantive challenge to the constitutional validity of the Aadhaar Act, 2016, its passage as a Money Bill under Article 110, and mandatory linkage of Aadhaar to bank accounts, mobile SIM cards, school admissions, and welfare subsidies.
issues: Is the Aadhaar Act constitutionally valid under the Puttaswamy privacy proportionality test?
Was the Aadhaar Act legitimately passed as a Money Bill?
ratio_decidendi: Upheld core biometric Aadhaar for government welfare subsidies under Section 7 (legitimate state aim of preventing leakage). Struck down Section 57 allowing private corporate entities to demand Aadhaar, mandatory bank account linking, mobile SIM linking, and school admissions. Upheld passage as Money Bill (Justice Chandrachud dissented).
verdict: Partially upheld Aadhaar for welfare subsidies; prohibited private corporate exploitation of Aadhaar database.

title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
case_name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
facts: Two girls were arrested in Maharashtra under Section 66A of the IT Act for posting comments on Facebook questioning the city shutdown for Bal Thackeray's funeral. Law student Shreya Singhal filed a PIL challenging Section 66A.
issues: Does Section 66A IT Act violate freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a)?
Is Section 66A unconstitutionally vague and overbroad?
ratio_decidendi: Section 66A created a chilling effect on free online speech. Differentiated between discussion, advocacy, and incitement. A speech becomes restriction-worthy under Article 19(2) only when it reaches the level of incitement. The terms 'grossly offensive' and 'annoying' were hopelessly vague. Read down Section 79 intermediary guidelines to require court orders or government notifications for takedowns.
verdict: Struck down Section 66A IT Act in its entirety as unconstitutional; protected internet freedom in India.

title: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020)
case_name: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
facts: Following the revocation of Article 370 in August 2019, the government imposed indefinite internet shutdown and movement restrictions under Section 144 CrPC across Jammu and Kashmir. Editor of Kashmir Times challenged the blackout.
issues: Is access to the internet a fundamental right under Article 19?
Can indefinite internet blackouts be imposed under Telecom Suspension Rules?
ratio_decidendi: Freedom of speech and expression (Article 19(1)(a)) and freedom to carry on trade/business (Article 19(1)(g)) using the medium of the internet are constitutionally protected fundamental rights. Indefinite internet suspensions are impermissible. All shutdown orders must satisfy proportionality and must be published proactively for judicial review.
verdict: Declared internet access constitutionally protected; prohibited indefinite shutdowns; mandated periodic review.

title: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974)

facts: Senior IAS officer E.P. Royappa was transferred from the post of Chief Secretary to a newly created non-cadre post, which he challenged as arbitrary, malicious, and violative of Articles 14 and 16.
issues: What is the conceptual scope of equality under Article 14?
Does Article 14 strike down arbitrary state action?
ratio_decidendi: Formulated the revolutionary 'New Doctrine of Equality'. title: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal Commission Case) (1992)
case_name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal Commission Case)
facts: V.P. Singh government implemented the Mandal Commission report reserving 27% vacancies in central civil services for Other Backward Classes (OBCs). Petitioners challenged the policy.
issues: Is caste alone a valid criterion for identifying backward classes?
What is the maximum permissible reservation ceiling?
Does reservation extend to promotions?
ratio_decidendi: Upheld 27% reservation for OBCs under Article 16(4). Caste can be an acceptable starting point for identifying backwardness. Established the 'Creamy Layer' exclusion principle for advanced sections of OBCs. Imposed a strict 50% ceiling on total reservations. Stated reservation applies only to initial appointments and not to promotions.
verdict: Upheld OBC reservation with creamy layer exclusion and 50% cap; prohibited reservation in promotions.

title: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1973)

facts: Government restricted import and quota of newsprint and imposed a 10-page ceiling on major daily newspapers (Times of India) under economic import regulations.

title: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (National Anthem Case) (1986)
case_name: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (National Anthem Case)
acts_referred: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
facts: Three school children belonging to Jehovah's Witnesses stood respectfully when the National Anthem was sung in school assembly, but did not sing along due to conscientious religious tenets. They were expelled.
issues: Does expulsion for respectfully standing without singing the National Anthem violate Articles 19(1)(a) and 25(1)?

title: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985)
case_name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
facts: 62-year-old divorced Muslim woman Shah Bano sought maintenance from her wealthy advocate husband under Section 125 CrPC. The husband argued Muslim personal law limited maintenance to the iddat period.
issues: Does Section 125 CrPC apply to divorced Muslim women notwithstanding personal law?
Is Section 125 secular in nature?
ratio_decidendi: Section 125 CrPC is a secular, compassionate statutory measure designed to prevent destitution and vagrancy. It applies to all citizens regardless of religion. It overrides personal laws where a divorced wife is unable to maintain herself. Highlighted the necessity of a Uniform Civil Code (Article 44).
verdict: Awarded maintenance to Shah Bano; affirmed secular primacy of Section 125 CrPC.

title: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (Triple Talaq Case) (2017)
case_name: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (Triple Talaq Case)
facts: Shayara Bano challenged the practice of Talaq-e-Biddat (instantaneous, irrevocable Triple Talaq pronounced in a single sitting) as violative of equality, non-discrimination, and dignity.
issues: Is Talaq-e-Biddat an essential religious practice protected under Article 25?
Is instant triple talaq manifestly arbitrary under Article 14?
ratio_decidendi: Talaq-e-Biddat is not an essential religious practice in Islamic theology. Justice Nariman held that instant triple talaq allows marital breakdown at the capricious whims of the husband without reconciliation, making it 'manifestly arbitrary' and void under Article 14.
verdict: Struck down Triple Talaq by 3:2 majority as unconstitutional; established manifest arbitrariness doctrine.

title: Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala Temple Case) (2018)
case_name: Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala Temple Case)
acts_referred: Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965
facts: Rule 3(b) of the Kerala rules prohibited entry of women aged 10 to 50 (menstruating age) into the Sabarimala Ayyappa temple based on the deity's celibate nature.
issues: Does excluding women aged 10-50 violate Articles 14, 15, and 25?
Is the exclusion an essential religious practice of the denomination under Article 26?
ratio_decidendi: Devotees of Lord Ayyappa do not constitute a separate religious denomination under Article 26. Excluding women on physiological attributes like menstruation is a form of untouchability and discrimination violating dignity and equality (Articles 14, 15, 21). Essential practice must be fundamental to the core faith. (Justice Indu Malhotra dissented).
verdict: Struck down Rule 3(b); permitted entry of women of all ages to Sabarimala temple.

title: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (Decriminalization of Section 377) (2018)
case_name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (Decriminalization of Section 377)
facts: LGBTQ+ activists challenged Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, which criminalized consensual sexual acts 'against the order of nature', following the retrograde reversal in Suresh Koushal (2013).
issues: Does criminalizing consensual adult same-sex intimacy violate Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21?
ratio_decidendi: Constitutional morality prevails over public/social morality. Consensual adult sexual intimacy in private is protected under privacy, personal autonomy, and dignity (Article 21). Discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited under Article 15(1) ('sex' includes sexual orientation).
verdict: Decriminalized consensual homosexual sex by reading down Section 377; recognized constitutional morality.

title: Joseph Shine v. Union of India (Decriminalization of Adultery) (2018)
case_name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India (Decriminalization of Adultery)
facts: Non-resident Indian Joseph Shine filed PIL challenging Section 497 IPC which punished a man for adultery with a married woman without consent of her husband, treating the woman as chattel of her husband.
issues: Does Section 497 IPC treat women as property of men, violating Articles 14, 15, and 21?
ratio_decidendi: Section 497 IPC is based on archaic patriarchal stereotypes reducing women to the chattel of their husbands. It punishes the outsider man while treating the woman as an object without agency, violating Article 14 and Article 15. Matrimonial infidelity is a civil ground for divorce, not a criminal offence under state penal sanctions.
verdict: Unanimously struck down Section 497 IPC and Section 198(2) CrPC as unconstitutional.

title: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case) (1981)
case_name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case)
facts: Challenge to government circular on non-appointment of additional High Court judges and mass transfers of High Court judges without concurrence of Chief Justice of India.
issues: Does 'consultation' in Articles 124 and 217 mean 'concurrence' of the Chief Justice of India?
ratio_decidendi: 'Consultation' does not mean 'concurrence'. The executive holds primacy in judicial appointments and transfers, provided there is full and effective consultation. Also established expansive rules of locus standi for Public Interest Litigation (PIL).

title: In re Special Reference No. 1 of 1998 (Third Judges Case) (1998)
case_name: In re Special Reference No. 1 of 1998 (Third Judges Case)
facts: President K.R. Narayanan sought an advisory opinion under Article 143 regarding the consultative process and collegium composition for appointing Supreme Court and High Court judges.
issues: What is the exact composition and quorum of the Collegium for judicial appointments and transfers?
ratio_decidendi: Expanded Collegium: For Supreme Court appointments, CJI must consult a collegium of 4 senior-most Supreme Court judges. For High Court appointments, CJI consults 2 senior-most judges. If majority of collegium advises against appointment, CJI shall not send recommendation.
verdict: Consolidated and institutionalized the 5-member Supreme Court Collegium framework.

title: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (NJAC Case / Fourth Judges) (2015)
case_name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (NJAC Case / Fourth Judges)
facts: Parliament unanimously enacted 99th Amendment and NJAC Act creating a 6-member Commission (CJI, 2 senior judges, Union Law Minister, and 2 eminent persons) with veto power to replace the Collegium.
issues: Does the inclusion of executive members in judicial selection infringe judicial independence as a Basic Feature?

title: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
case_name: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
facts: Challenge to constitutional validity of Article 323A(2)(d) and Section 28 of Administrative Tribunals Act which excluded the jurisdiction of High Courts under Articles 226/227 over administrative tribunal decisions.
issues: Can Parliament exclude High Court writ jurisdiction over tribunals?
Is judicial review under Articles 226 and 32 part of the Basic Structure?
ratio_decidendi: Power of judicial review vested in High Courts under Article 226/227 and Supreme Court under Article 32 is an integral part of the Basic Structure. Tribunals are supplemental bodies; all decisions of tribunals are subject to supervisory scrutiny of a Division Bench of the High Court.
verdict: Declared exclusion of High Court writ jurisdiction over tribunals unconstitutional; saved judicial review.

title: State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor of Punjab (2023)
case_name: State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor of Punjab
facts: Governor of Punjab refused to grant assent to multiple bills passed by the Vidhan Sabha, claiming the speaker's reconvening of the budget session was illegal and withholding assent indefinitely.
issues: Can a Governor withhold assent indefinitely under Article 200 without returning bills to the Assembly?

A Governor is a symbolic constitutional head and cannot veto democratic legislation.
verdict: Mandated that Governors act promptly; prohibited indefinite pocket-vetoes of state legislation.

title: In re Article 370 of the Constitution (2023)
case_name: In re Article 370 of the Constitution
acts_referred: Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Orders C.O. 272 and C.O. 273
facts: Challenge to the abrogating Presidential Orders C.O. 272 and C.O. 273 of August 2019 which rendered Article 370 inoperative and bifurcated Jammu and Kashmir into two Union Territories.
issues: Was Article 370 permanent or temporary?

title: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987)
case_name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case)
facts: Severe leak of hazardous Oleum gas from Shriram Foods and Fertilizer plant in Delhi shortly after the Bhopal disaster, causing deaths and mass panic. M.C. Mehta filed PIL under Article 32.
issues: What is the standard of liability for hazardous and inherently dangerous industrial enterprises?
ratio_decidendi: Evolved the landmark 'Absolute Liability' doctrine, discarding the 19th-century English Rylands v. Fletcher strict liability with its exceptions. An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community. Compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and financial capacity of the enterprise.

title: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (Pavement Dwellers Case) (1985)
case_name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (Pavement Dwellers Case)
facts: BMC initiated eviction of pavement and slum dwellers from Bombay footpaths without notice or alternative rehabilitation during monsoon rains.
issues: Does the right to life under Article 21 include the right to livelihood?
ratio_decidendi: The right to livelihood is an integral facet of the right to life under Article 21. If the right to livelihood is not treated as part of the right to life, the easiest way of depriving a person of his life would be to deprive him of his means of livelihood. Eviction cannot be executed without notice and reasonable opportunity of being heard.
verdict: Recognized Right to Livelihood in Article 21; mandated fair notice and phased alternative housing.

title: Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013)

title: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (Electoral Bonds Case) (2024)
case_name: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (Electoral Bonds Case)
facts: Government introduced Electoral Bonds Scheme 2018 permitting anonymous, unlimited political contributions by corporations and individuals without public disclosure.
issues: Does unlimited anonymous political funding infringe voter's right to information under Article 19(1)(a)?

title: Sita Soren v. Union of India (Legislative Bribery Immunity Case) (2024)
case_name: Sita Soren v. Union of India (Legislative Bribery Immunity Case)
facts: JMM MLA Sita Soren was accused of accepting a bribe to vote for an independent candidate in Rajya Sabha elections. She claimed constitutional immunity under Article 194(2) relying on P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
issues: Does parliamentary privilege protect MPs/MLAs from criminal prosecution for accepting bribes to speak or vote?
ratio_decidendi: Parliamentary privilege under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) exists to foster deliberative democratic independence, not to confer exemption from ordinary criminal law.
